intro: The summit weather station has been automated for forty years, yet the forecasters still keep a chair warm by the single window where the anemometer ticks against the glass. This morning the printer woke with a long, papery sigh and fed out a sheet that was definitely not a forecast: no isobars, no fronts, just a block of quiet symbols that made the coffee taste of copper. Old Mara did not call the met office; she only poured a second cup and watched the barometer's brass flag shiver once, as if it recognised a handwriting it had waited decades to see. Outside, the ridge kept holding its breath, and the printer began to hum again before anyone dared to say what day it was. By lunch the charts were back on the wall, pinned a little crooked against the howling glass, and the printer stayed silent as if it were waiting for a proper question.
echo: The Arabic word meant simply 'season', and here the season means rain.

puzzles.title: Occluded Front
puzzles.flavor: Pairs of numbers pencilled in the margin.

blocks.text: The weather station on the summit has been automated for forty years. This morning its printer woke up and produced something that is definitely not a forecast.

hints: The first number in each pair never goes past the number of words on the page. What does the second count?

puzzles.title: Squall Line
puzzles.flavor: The sprocket keeps count; the holes do the talking. Half a turn of the wheel and you'd have it.

partials.4f6d4f40440bb4fc9c4bf1e3ad0835e149bc0e8c: You've decoded it, but it's not finished. One more layer.

hints: Seven positions a row, each punched or not. What were seven bits once enough for? And if what you get still isn't a word, reread the flavour text.

puzzles.title: Shipping Forecast
puzzles.flavor: The Senate admitted only the indivisible.
hints: Read the numerals. They're all prime. Is there a natural way to number the primes?

puzzles.title: Beaufort Twelve
puzzles.flavor: Everything fell straight down, and landed in the right column.
hints: Black squares are spaces. Which two- and three-letter words fit, using only the letters each column allows?

puzzles.title: Wind Chill
puzzles.flavor: The words are nonsense. The typesetting isn't.
hints: Two kinds of letter, big and small. How many of them would you need to spell twenty-six different things?

puzzles.title: Inversion
puzzles.flavor: Three letters to a strip, and a note of how long each word was.
hints: The strips are alphabetised, not in order. The word lengths say where the breaks fall. Which strip could start the sentence?

meta.title: Meta: Isobars
meta.flavor: Every report is signed with a single initial. Blaise would know what to do with them.
hints: Blaise de Vigenère needed a key to open this. Has every answer signed its work?
